la:other:Cassius.html:
Cassĭus, a
old form Casseius; hence, Cassīus, and from this Cassĭus is formed; cf. Ritschl de Sepulcro Fur.
,
the name of a Roman gens; esp. distinguished,
L. Cassius Longinus Ravilla, a very severe judge; from him the Lex tabellaria Cassia proceeded, A. U. C. 617, by which the judges were obliged to vote with little tablets, ; ; ; ; and .—
Hence, Cassĭānus, a, um, adj., of Cassius, ; .—
The consul L. Cassius, who, A.U.C. 647, was conquered and slain by the Helvetii, and 12.—Hence, bellum Cassianum, .—

C. Cassius Longinus, a distinguished jurist under Claudius; his adherents were Cassiani and Cassiana schola, ; ; .—
After a Cassius not now known was named the Cassia Via, a branch of the Via Flaminia, ; cf. Paul. ex Müll.

cascus, a, um, adj.

,

senses: several soldiers' tents situated together; hence, a military camp, an encampment
la:noun:castrum.html:
castrum, i, n.
kindred with casa, q. v.
.
In sing., any fortified place; a castle, fort, fortress (more rare than castellum): ei Grunium dederat in Phrygiā castrum, etc.,; . 29, 4; —
Esp., nom. propr.
Castrum Altum or Album, in Hispania Tarraconensis, .—
Castrum Inui, or simply Castrum, an ancient city of the Rutuli, near Ardea, ; called Castrum,; . —
Castrum Novum, a city on the seacoast of Etruria, ; .—
Another Castrum Novum, on the sea-coast of Picenum, now Giulia Nova,

; also called absol. Castrum, .—

Castrum Truentinum, a maritime city of Picenum, on the river Truentus, , B, 1; also called Truentum,.—
Castrum Vergium, a fortress of the Bergistani in Hispania Tarraconensis, now Berga, .—Far more freq.,
In plur.: castra, ōrum, n. (castra, ae, f.: castra haec vestra est, Att. ap. ; Trag. Rel. p. 238 Rib.).
Lit., several soldiers' tents situated together; hence, a military camp, an encampment; among the Romans a square (quadrata); later, after the manner of the Greeks, sometimes circular, or adjusted to its situation,. It was surrounded by a trench (fossa) and a wall (vallum), and had four gates: Porta Praetoria, the front, chief gate, on the opp. side from the enemy, from which the legions marched; opp. to this, Porta Decumana (in later times Porta Quaestoria), the back gate; Porta Principalis Dextra, and Porta Principalis Sinistra, situated on the two sides of the camp,; cf. Dict. of Antiq.—
Phrases.
With adj.: stativa,occupied for a long time, permanent,; ; ; ; : aestiva,summer camp,; : hiberna, (more freq. absol. aestiva and hiberna, q. v.): navalia,an encampment on the shore for protecting the fleet and the troops while landing; sometimes connected with the ships drawn to land, Herz.; cf. ; ; called also nautica,; (cf. § 4; ): lunata, crescent-shaped, Auct. B. Afr. 80.—With numerals: una,: bina,; : quina,.—
With verb: locum castris antecapere,; cf.: capere locum castris,; ; and montes castris capere,: castra metari, Cael. ap. ; ; : facere,; ; : ponere,; ; : ponere et munire,: munire,; : communire,; : castra castris conferre,; : castris se tenere,: castra movere,to break up, to decamp,fin.; also syn. with to march forth from a camp, Herz.; 1, 22; 2, 2; ; ; et saep.—Hence, also, promovere, : movere retro,: removere,: proferre,: castris castra inferre, Vahl.—
Castra Praetoriana, Praetoria, Urbana or simply Castra, the barracks of the Prœtorians in the suburbs of Rome, ; ; ; ; ; . —
Castrorum filius, a surname of Caligula, who was brought up in the camp, ; .—So, Castrorum mater, an appellation of Faustina, the wife of the emperor Marcus Aurelius, because she accompanied him in an expedition against the Quadi, .—Hence both appell. in later inscriptions as titles of the Roman emperors and empresses.—
Esp. as nom. propr., like castrum.
Castra Corneliana or Cornelia, on the north coast of Africa, near Utica, so called because the elder Scipio Africanus first pitched his camp there, after his landing in Africa, in the second Punic war, ; ; ; ; .—
Castra Caecilia, in Lusitania, .—
Castra Hannibalis, a seaport town in Bruttium, .—
Castra Pyrrhi, a place in Grecian Illyria, .—
Castra Vetera or Vetera, a place on the Lower Rhine, now Xanthen, ; ; ; .—
Castra Alexandri, a district in Egypt, ; .—
Meton.
Since, in military expeditions, a camp was pitched each evening, in the histt. (esp. Livy) for a day's march: secundis castris ( = bidui itinere) pervenit ad Dium,; so ; cf.: alteris castris,; .— So tertiis castris,; ; : quartis castris,: quintis castris,; : septimis castris,: decimis castris,; .—
Military service (hence, often opp. forum and toga), ; ; : qui magnum in castris usum habebant,.—
Of beehives: cerea,: in apium castris,.—
Of a sheepfold, .—
Of political parties, regarded as arrayed in hostility: si ad interdicti sententiam confugis... in meis castris praesidiisque versaris,.—
Of philosophical sects: Epicuri castra,: O castra praeclara (Epicuri)!; ; .

la:verb:castro.html:
castro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
Sanscr. çastra, knife, sword
.
To deprive of generative power (both of male and female), to emasculate, castrate, geld: hircum, and 4: agnum,: gallos,; ; ; : sues,; ; —
Transf. to plants, to prune, lop, trim, ; ; .—
Trop.: vina saccis, to pass through a sack or bag, to filter, ; cf. : siligo castrata,i. e. cleaned,: semen,.—
In gen., to shorten, cut off, curtail: caudas catulorum,; cf. : alvos apum,to take up, to take out the honey,; ; cf.: castrare alvearia,.—
Trop., to enervate, debilitate: castrata res publica morte Africani, weakened (a vulgar figure, acc. to ; ): nisi illum (Maecenatem) enervasset felicitas, immo castrasset,: libellos,to remove obscenity, to expurgate,: vires,to diminish,: avaritiam,to check, restrain,.

cassis, ĭdis (access. form cassĭda, ae, like chlamyda from chlamys, ; ; cf. Prob. II. p. 1473 P. Lind.; P.; ib. Also Paul. ex , instead of cassilam, the reading should be cassidam), f.
Etruscan, acc. to ; cf. Müll. Etrusk. 1, p. 392; cf. Sanscr. khad, to cover, and Lat. castrum, casa
,
a helmet, commonly of metal (as galea was of leather, ; cf. ), ; ; ; : fracta,: caelata,.—But also promiscuously for galea, (cf.: aerea galea,).—

la:adj:cassus.html:
cassus, a, um, adj.,
empty, void, hollow.
Prop. (syn.: inanis, vacuus; mostly poet.).
Absol.: nux,; : glans,: canna,unfruitful,: granum inane cassumque,: anulus, Fab. Pict. ap. . 6.—Subst.: palearum cassa, Sol. c. 52 fin.—
Expressing that of which the subject is empty, etc., wanting, devoid of, deprived of, without.
With abl.: sanguine cassa (cochlea), bloodless, Poët. ap. ; so, virgo dote cassa,: lumine aër,: lumine corpus,; : animā corpus,.—Poet.: cassus lumine (= vitā),deprived of life, dead,; imitated by ; and in like sense aethere cassus,: simulacra cassa sensu,.—
With gen.: cassus luminis ensis,.—
With ab: elementum ab omnibus,.—
Trop., vain, empty, useless, futile, fruitless (syn.: inanis, irritus): cassum quiddam et inani vocis sono decoratum, * ; so, copia verborum,: vota,: fertilitas terrae,: fraus,: consilia,: viae,vain, profitless,: labores,: manus,without effect,: augur futuri,false, erring,: omen,.—Subst.: cassa, ōrum, n., empty things: palearum,; esp. of speech: cassa memorare,to talk idly,; so, cassa habebantur quae, etc.,were thought vain, futile,; .— Esp. freq. in poetry (in prose, but not in Cic.), in cassum, or, in one word, incas-sum, adverb., in vain, uselessly, to no purpose: ex multis omnia in cassum cadunt,; cf. : temere, in cassum frustraque, without aim or purpose, fortuitously, ; so ; : furere,: longos ciebat Incassum fletus,: tot incassum fusos patiere labores?.—In prose: quae profecto incassum agebantur, Dietsch: vana incassum jactare tela,: incassum missae preces,: aliquid incassum disserere,; ; ; : frustra in cassumque. .— Also cassum: quid cassum times? Sen. Herc. Oet. 353; cf.: μάτην, frustra, nequicquam, cassum, Gloss. Cyrill.

la:other:Casus.html:
cāsus (Ciceronis temporibus paulumque infra s geminabatur: cassus, etc., ; cf.: causa, Juppiter al.; in inscr. also KASVS), ūs (dat. casu, ), m.
cado
.
Lit., a falling (acc. to cado, I. A. and C.).
A falling down, etc.: stillicidi,: geli,: nivis,: fulminum,; : celsae graviore casu Decidunt turres,.—In plur., .—
A fall, an overthrow, a throwing down: occumbunt multi letum praecipe casu, Vahl.: eoque ictu me ad casum dari, Att. ap. : casus, quo (infantes) in terram toties deferuntur,; : vehiculi,—In plur.: cum loci Inciperent casus, i. e. the fall, destruction (by an earthquake), .—
Trop.
Of time, the end: extremae sub casum hiemis,.—
A moral fall, a false step, an error, fall: multas vias adulescentiae lubricas ostendit (natura), quibus illa insistere, aut ingredi sine casu aliquo ac prolapsione vix posset,.—So of a political fall, .—
Esp., a fall or change from a higher to a lower condition: secum reputans quam gravis casus in servitium ex regno foret,.—
That which turns out or happens unexpectedly, an occurrence, event, accident, chance, misfortune, emergency (this most freq. in sing. and plur.): quid est enim aliud fors, quid fortuna, quid casus, quid eventus, nisi cum sic aliquid cecidit, sic evenit, ut vel non cadere atque evenire, vel aliter cadere atque evenire potuerit? etc.,: quis iste tantus casus? unde tam felix concursus atomorum? cf. : novi casus temporum,: quod consilium etsi in ejusmodi casu reprehendendum non est, tamen incommode accidit,such an emergency,: quod in ejusmodi casu accidit, periti ignaris parebant,; ; ; ; ; : potest igitur veritatem

casus imitari, : quis tantam Rutulis laudem, casusne deusne, Attulerit,: sive illud deorum munus sive casus fuit,: quae casus obtulerat, in sapientiam vertenda ratus,: ut quemque casus armaverat,: si quos locus aut casus conjunxerat,: in aleam tanti casus se regnumque dare,: ludibrium casūs,: casum potius quam consilium sequatur,: parata ad omnes casus eloquentia,: bellorum,: satis jam eventuum, satis casuum,: adversi, secundi,; cf. ; : magnus,; Planc. ap. : mirificus,: mirabiles,: rariores,: dubii,; : varii,: subiti repentinique,.—Hence, in abl.: casu, adverbially, by chance, casually, by accident, accidentally: quod si haec habent aliquam talem necessitatem, quid est tandem, quod casu fieri aut forte fortunā putemus?: id evenit non temere nec casu,: sive casu sive consilio deorum,; cf. : necessitate an casu,: casu an persuasu et inductu,: casu an manibus impeditus,: accidit casu ut legati, etc.,; cf. ; ; ; ; ; et saep.—Hence, also,

A chance, an occasion, opportunity for something (esp. freq. in Sall. and Tac.): aetas illa multo pluris quam nostra casus mortis habet,; cf.: mortis durae casus,: aut vi aut dolis sese casum victoriae inventurum,: praeclari facinoris casum dare,; so, si casus daretur,; : invadendae Armeniae,: pugnae,: bene gerendae rei,: casum adferre,.— Since the idea of suddenness, unexpectedness, easily passes into that of hostility, adverseness (cf. accido, 4.), casus signifies,
Esp., an adverse event, a misfortune, mishap, calamity, = συμφορά: meum illum casum tam horribilem, tam gravem, tam repentinum,; ; : dolens civitatis casum,; cf. ; ; ; ; .—Of disease: si alius casus lecto te adfixit,; ; ; : res minime in hujusmodi casu noxia,in the earthquake,; : urbis Trojanae,overthrow,.—Hence,
Euphemist. for death: Saturnini atque Gracchorum casus,: sui quemque casus per quinquennium absumpsissent,; ; ; ; cf. ; .—
In gram. t. t., a case in the inflection of words: propter eorum qui dicunt, sunt declinati casus, uti is qui de altero diceret, distinguere posset, quom vocaret, etc., Müll.: casus dicimus... et vocabulorum formas, Paul. ex ib.: ea (verba) sic et casibus et temporibus et genere et numero conservemus, ut, etc.,: barbari casus... casus rectus,; : obliqui,: nominativo, dativo, ablativo,: genitivo,: Latinus, sextus, i. e. the ablative, Varr. ap. P.: conversi, i. e. obliqui,: interrogandi (i. e. genetivus), Nigid. ap. Hertz: vocandi,: septimus,.

a structure in which the water of an aqueduct is collected, to be distributed by pipes or channels in different directions; a reservoir
la:noun:castellum.html:
castellum, i, n.dim.
castrum
,
a castle, fort, citadel, fortress, stronghold, Sisenn. ap. ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; also of a single bulwark, bastion, ; ; ; ; and poet. of a dwelling in an elevated position, .—
In mechanics, a structure in which the water of an aqueduct is collected, to be distributed by pipes or channels in different directions, a reservoir, ; ; ; ; ; —
Trop., shelter, stronghold, defence, refuge (cf. arx, I. B.): templum Castoris fuit arx civium perditorum... castellum forensis latrocinii,: urbem philosophiae, mihi crede, proditis, dum castella defendis,: tribunal Appii castellum omnium scelerum,.

la:verb:castigo.html:
castīgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
castum-ago, as purgo = purum-ago
,
to set right by word or deed, to correct, chastise, punish; to blame, reprove, chide, censure, find fault with (syn.: animadvertere, punire; more forcible than reprehendere and vituperare; weaker than culpare; class. in prose and poetry): pueros non verbis solum, sed etiam verberibus,; so, verberibus,; cf. ; : magnā clade,: baculo,: quo saepius (magister) monuerit, hoc rarius castigabit,: laudat Pompeius... segniores castigat atque incitat,; so opp. laudare,; : castigando increpandoque plus quam leniter agendo, proficere,: servos exuviis bubulis,: aliquem dictis plurumis,; : verbis,; : litteris,: per litteras,: leniter,; : vehementissime,: in hoc me ipse castigo quod, etc.,: segnitiem hominum atque inertiam,; : nimiam lenitatem,: moras,: dolos,: vitia,; ; —
Esp.
To correct some error, to set right, mend (poet. or in post-Aug. prose) ( = corrigere, emendare): carmen, *: amicae verba,: examen improbum in trutină,: vitia sua,.—
To hold in check, to restrain; lit. and trop. (rare for the more usu. coërcere, cohibere, etc.): quid illum credis facturum, nisi eum ... servas, castigas, mones?: equum tenacem, non parentem frenis asperioribus castigare,; : castigatus animi dolor,: risum crebris potiunculis,: lapsus,; cf. under P. a.—Hence,
Of relations of space, to enclose, surround, encompass, confine, shut in: insula castigatur aquis,.— Hence, castīgātus, a, um, P. a. (poet. or in post-Aug. prose), confined, compressed; hence,
As a designation of physical beauty, small, slender, close: pectus,: frons,.—
Trop., restrained, checked: luxuria tanto castigatior, quanto posset esse liberior, , 5, 24: castigatissima disciplina,the strictest, Hertz (Cod. Reg. castissima).—Adv.: castīgātē.

la:adj:castus.html:
castus, a, um, adj.
i. e. cas-tus, partic., kindr. to Sanscr. çludh, to cleanse; Gr. καθ-αρός; Germ. keusch, heiter; cf. the opp. in-ces-tus, impure, Bopp, Gloss. 351, 6; Pott. 1, 252
.
In gen., morally pure, unpolluted, spotless, guiltless, = purus, integer (gen. in respect to the person himself, while candidus signifies pure, just, in respect to other men; v. Doed. Syn. p. 196 sq.; class. in prose and poetry): castus animus purusque,; cf.: vita purissima et castissima,; and: quis hoc adulescente castior? quis modestior? quis autem illo qui maledicit impurior?: perjurum castus (fraudasse dicatur),: castissimum quoque hominem ad peccandum potuisse impellere,: nulli fas casto sceleratum insistere limen,: populus Et frugi castusque verecundusque,: qui (animi) se integros castosque servavissent,; cf. ; : M. Crassi castissima domus,: signa,signs, indications of innocence,: fides,inviolable,: Saguntum,.—With ab: decet nos esse a culpā castos,; so, res familiaris casta a cruore civili,.—
In respect to particular virtues.
Most freq., esp. in poetry, in regard to sexual morality, pure, chaste, unpolluted, virtuous, continent: Latona, Vahl.; cf. Minerva,; ; ; ; ; : hostia = Iphigenia,: Bellerophon,: matres,: maritae,.— With ab: castus ab rebus venereis,.—Of inanimate things: lectulus,: cubile,: flos virginis,: gremium,: vultus,: domus,; —
Trop., of style, free from barbarisms, pure: Caius Caesar sermonis praeter alios suae aetatis castissimi,.—
In a religious respect, pious, religious, holy, sacred, = pius: hac casti maneant in religione nepotes, Wagn.— So, Aeneas (for which elsewhere pius in Verg.),: sacerdotes,: et sanctus princeps,: ego qui castam contionem, sanctum campum defendo (in respect to the preceding: in Campo Martio, comitiis centuriatis auspicato in loco),.—Of things: sacrae, religiosae castaeque res, Varr. ap. : haud satis castum donum deo,; cf. festa,: taedae, Serv.: ara castis Vincta verbenis,: crines,: laurus,: castior amnis (sc. Musarum),; cf.: castum flumen (on account of the nymphs),: luci,: nemus,: pura castaque mens,: casta mola genus sacrificii, quod Vestales virgines faciebant, Paul. ex Müll.—As epith. ornans of poetry, since it is used in defence of the Deity: casta poesis, Varr. ap. (it is erroneously explained by Non. by suavis, jucundus).—
Hence, subst.: castum, i, n., a festival, or period of time consecrated to a god, during which strict continence was enjoined, Müll.: Isidis et Cybeles,.—
In respect to the property and rights of others, free from, abstinent, disinterested: manus, Varr. ap. : homo castus ac non cupidus,: castissimus homo atque integerrimus,.—Adv.: castē.
(Acc. to I.) Purely, spotlessly, without stain, uprightly: agere aetatem suam,: et integre vivere,; .—
(Acc. to II. A.) Chastely, virtuously: caste se habere a servis, C. Gracch. ap. : tueri eloquentiam ut adultam virginem,.—Of language, properly, correctly, classically: caste pureque linguā Latinā uti,.—
(Acc. to II. B.) Piously, religiously: placare deos,; cf. ; .—Comp., .—Sup., .
